subject: Art & Design
title: Wayfinding Typography: Signs That Save Lives
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Wayfinding Typography: Signs That Save Lives.

hook.text: At 70 mph, you have 3 seconds to read a highway sign. The wrong font could mean a missed exit — or a crash.

buildup.text: Wayfinding typography guides people through airports, hospitals, highways, and cities using signs and symbols.

discovery.text: Highway Gothic (US) and Transport (UK) were designed for maximum legibility at speed and distance.

twist.text: In 2004, the US replaced Highway Gothic with Clearview — then reversed the decision in 2016. Font choice is political.

climax.text: Hospital wayfinding saves lives. A patient who can't find the ER because of bad signage faces real danger.

punchline.text: Some typography isn't about beauty. It's about survival.

quiz.question: Why is font choice critical for highway signage?
options: Drivers have only seconds to read signs at high speed — legibility is life-or-death
Governments want signs to look decorative
Highways only allow one specific font by law

details.summary: Wayfinding typography designs signage systems for navigation — airports, hospitals, highways, transit systems. These typefaces must be instantly legible at distance, under stress, and in poor lighting.
details.whyItMatters: Wayfinding typography has the highest stakes in the field — a misread hospital sign or highway exit can endanger lives. It demonstrates that typography's most important function isn't beauty but clarity when clarity matters most.
takeaways: Wayfinding type must be legible at distance and under stress
Airport, highway, and hospital signage demands life-critical clarity
Function and legibility take absolute priority over expression

faq.question: What makes a font good for highway signs?
faq.answer: Large x-height for distance readability, open counters that resist fill-in from headlight reflection, mixed case (easier to read than ALL CAPS at speed), high stroke contrast for nighttime visibility, and generous spacing.

faq.question: Why does the London Underground font matter?
faq.answer: Edward Johnston's 1916 typeface for London Underground was one of the first commissioned corporate typefaces and one of the earliest sans-serif designs for wayfinding. It established that public signage required specially designed type.
